title: Performative Allyship and the Sincerity Problem

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Current critiques of performative allyship conflate genuine but misguided support with deliberate self-serving behavior, creating unfair skepticism toward well-intentioned allies
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Distinguish between mimetic allyship (copying ally behaviors without understanding) and strategic allyship (deliberate image management), showing each requires different responses
core_contribution.significance: Provides more nuanced framework for evaluating ally behavior and avoiding counterproductive blanket dismissals of imperfect support

novelty.what_is_new: First systematic analysis separating different motivational structures underlying apparently performative ally behavior
novelty.why_publishable: Resolves persistent debates about ally authenticity by providing clearer conceptual distinctions
novelty.why_achievable: Uses familiar examples and straightforward conceptual analysis without requiring extensive empirical research

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Basic conceptual analysis using intention-action frameworks
key_assumptions: Actions can be evaluated by motivational structure
Allyship involves both internal commitment and external action
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Recent work on performativity, virtue signaling, and solidarity in feminist philosophy and philosophy of race

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Clear behavioral patterns that can be analyzed through standard philosophical tools for examining motivation and action
development_risks: Risk of seeming to excuse harmful behavior
Need to balance theoretical precision with practical applicability

title: The Autonomy Paradox in Content Moderation

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Platform content moderation creates a paradox where protecting user autonomy requires restricting user autonomy, but current analyses fail to distinguish between different autonomy interests at stake
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Separate immediate choice autonomy from reflective autonomy, showing that content curation can enhance reflective autonomy even while constraining immediate choices
core_contribution.significance: Provides framework for evaluating content policies that moves beyond simple freedom-restriction trade-offs

novelty.what_is_new: Novel application of autonomy distinctions to digital platform governance, revealing hidden conceptual structure
novelty.why_publishable: Advances both autonomy theory and applied ethics of technology through precise conceptual work
novelty.why_achievable: Builds on established autonomy concepts and uses clear real-world examples without requiring technical expertise

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Standard autonomy analysis from moral and political philosophy
key_assumptions: Some restrictions can enhance rather than diminish autonomy
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Classical autonomy theory, recent work on digital ethics and platform governance

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Well-established autonomy concepts applied to concrete digital scenarios with clear practical implications
development_risks: Need to avoid technical details about algorithms

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Debates about who can take offense on behalf of others lack clarity about what grounds moral standing to be offended, leading to inconsistent judgments about borrowed offense
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Distinguish between relational standing (based on relationships to affected parties) and structural standing (based on position within relevant social structures)
core_contribution.significance: Provides principled framework for evaluating when borrowed offense is legitimate versus overreach

novelty.what_is_new: First systematic analysis of the grounds for moral standing in offense-taking, revealing overlooked complexity
novelty.why_publishable: Addresses widespread social phenomenon through rigorous conceptual analysis
novelty.why_achievable: Uses clear examples and established concepts from moral philosophy without requiring extensive background

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Basic moral standing analysis and conceptual distinction-drawing
key_assumptions: Not everyone has equal standing to be offended by everything
Standing can be earned or derived from relationships
Moral emotions can be appropriate or inappropriate
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Work on moral standing, moral emotions, and group-differentiated harms

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Observable social behaviors that can be analyzed using familiar moral philosophical tools
development_risks: Politically sensitive topic requiring careful handling
Risk of oversimplifying complex social dynamics

title: Aesthetic Testimony and the Limits of Deference

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Standard accounts of aesthetic testimony fail to explain why deferring to critics feels epistemically appropriate but aesthetically unsatisfying
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Aesthetic knowledge requires experiential acquaintance in a way that creates rational pressure to seek direct experience even when testimony is reliable
core_contribution.significance: Explains the distinctive epistemic structure of aesthetic domains and why aesthetic testimony feels different from other forms of expert testimony

novelty.what_is_new: Identifies unique feature of aesthetic epistemology that distinguishes it from standard testimony cases
novelty.why_publishable: Resolves puzzling asymmetry in our attitudes toward aesthetic experts using rigorous conceptual analysis
novelty.why_achievable: Uses familiar examples and established epistemological concepts without requiring technical apparatus

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Basic epistemological analysis of testimony and knowledge types
key_assumptions: Different domains may have different epistemic structures
Knowledge and understanding can come apart
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Recent work on aesthetic testimony, epistemic value of experience, and testimony more generally

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Clear intuitive phenomenon that can be analyzed using well-established epistemological distinctions
development_risks: Need to avoid overgeneralizing about aesthetic experience
Risk of conflating different types of aesthetic judgment
distinctive_advantages: Addresses puzzle many readers will recognize
Contributes to both epistemology and aesthetics

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Binary complicity judgments fail to capture the moral reality that complicit agents experience different degrees and types of moral residue depending on their level of involvement
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Develop gradational account of complicity that tracks different contribution types and explains corresponding variations in moral residue and remedial obligations
core_contribution.significance: Provides more nuanced framework for assessing complicit agents moral status and forward-looking obligations

novelty.what_is_new: First systematic account linking degrees of complicity to patterns of moral residue and remedial obligation
novelty.why_publishable: Advances complicity theory by explaining previously unanalyzed moral phenomena
novelty.why_achievable: Builds on existing complicity literature using clear examples and conceptual analysis

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Standard moral philosophical analysis of complicity, responsibility, and moral emotions
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Recent work on complicity, collective responsibility, and moral emotions
background_knowledge: Moral psychology of guilt and responsibility

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Well-defined moral phenomena that can be analyzed using established tools from moral philosophy
development_risks: Complexity of mapping contribution types to moral residue
Need to avoid overly complex taxonomies
distinctive_advantages: Connects theory to lived moral experience

core_contribution.conceptual_issue: Accounts of empathy assume stable identity boundaries, but transformative empathetic experiences can alter the empathizer in ways that blur the self-other distinction
core_contribution.proposed_solution: Distinguish between projective empathy (maintaining identity boundaries) and incorporative empathy (allowing identity boundary shifts), showing each has different epistemic and ethical properties
core_contribution.significance: Explains why some empathetic experiences feel identity-threatening while others feel identity-preserving, with implications for empathy ethics

novelty.what_is_new: First analysis of how empathy can transform rather than merely inform the empathizer, challenging standard empathy models
novelty.why_publishable: Identifies overlooked feature of empathetic experience with implications for empathy theory and ethics
novelty.why_achievable: Uses recognizable examples and established concepts from philosophy of mind and ethics

scope_assessment.technical_requirements: Basic conceptual analysis of empathy, personal identity, and moral psychology
key_assumptions: Different empathy types have different properties
scope_assessment.literature_engagement: Recent work on empathy, transformative experience, and personal identity

viability_assessment.conceptual_clarity: Identifiable psychological phenomenon that can be analyzed using standard philosophical tools
development_risks: Need to avoid overly psychological focus
Risk of conflating empathy with other phenomena
distinctive_advantages: Has practical implications for moral education
